questions.q: Why does raw work order data land in a staging table instead of going straight into the warehouse?
options: A staging table gives a bad load somewhere safe to fail, separates extraction from transformation, and doesn't put the live SSRS/Power BI-facing warehouse tables at risk
SQL Server requires all data to pass through a staging table before it can be queried
AdventureWorks2012 has no way to query Production.WorkOrder directly
Staging tables are faster to query than warehouse tables
questions.explain: This is the same staging discipline Data Modeling & Data Warehousing's Chapter 5 taught: staging exists as a buffer so a bad load fails somewhere safe, not against tables already in production use.

questions.q: Why is stg.WorkOrder built with VARCHAR columns and no constraints instead of matching Production.WorkOrder's real data types?
options: So a load never fails because of a data type mismatch — validation and conversion happen downstream, against data that's already safely landed
Because VARCHAR is always faster to query than INT or DATE
Because Production.WorkOrder itself only stores VARCHAR data
Because staging tables are not allowed to have any columns at all
questions.explain: Loosely-typed, unconstrained staging tables accept whatever the source sends without the load itself failing — fixing data type problems is deferred to the transform step.

questions.q: Which schema does the staging table live in, and why is it kept separate from the warehouse schema?
options: The stg schema — kept separate from dw so the warehouse's strict, constrained tables aren't mixed with staging's loose, disposable ones, even on the same SQL Server instance
The dbo schema — SQL Server has no concept of separate schemas
The dw schema — staging tables always live alongside warehouse tables
Staging tables cannot be placed in any schema
questions.explain: stg and dw are separate schemas on the same instance — Lesson 5 explains this separation in full, but the schema is created here.

questions.q: What does this lesson's work set up for Lesson 4's SSIS package to actually do?
options: Give WorkOrderETL.dtsx's first Data Flow Task a real OLE DB Destination to write into — the empty stg schema and stg.WorkOrder table
Nothing — Lesson 4 creates its own tables independently
It fully populates the warehouse fact and dimension tables
It replaces the need for an SSIS package entirely
questions.explain: After this lesson, stg.WorkOrder exists but is empty. Lesson 4's Data Flow Task 1 is what actually moves rows into it.

questions.q: Which real AdventureWorks2012 column on Production.WorkOrder will eventually resolve to a role-playing DimDate foreign key, not a regular dimension?
options: StartDate, EndDate, and DueDate
WorkOrderID
ProductID
OrderQty
questions.explain: StartDate, EndDate, and DueDate are the three milestone dates that Lesson 6 resolves into three separate role-playing foreign keys, all pointing at the same physical DimDate table.
